## Station Overview

The **Time Warp** station investigates how accurately we perceive time and physical dimensions. Participants estimate a 60-second interval, visually estimate line lengths, tactilely estimate string lengths (with eyes closed), and guess the room temperature. This station generates **error scores** that reveal systematic biases in human perception.

## What Participants Do

### Part A: 60-Second Estimation
1. Close your eyes
2. When your partner says "Start", sense time passing
3. Say "Stop" when you think **60 seconds** have passed
4. Partner records the actual time elapsed

### Part B: Visual Estimation (Lines)
1. Look at **Line Card A** — estimate its length in cm
2. Repeat with **Line Card B**

### Part C: Tactile Estimation (Strings)
1. Feel **String 1** with eyes closed — estimate its length in cm
2. Repeat with **String 2**

### Part D: Temperature Estimation
1. Guess the current room temperature in °C

## Research Questions

> Do people systematically over- or under-estimate 60 seconds?

> Is visual estimation more accurate than tactile estimation?

> Does counting during time estimation improve accuracy?

## Experimental Design

| Element | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Design | Within-groups (multiple estimation tasks) |
| IV | Estimation modality (time, visual, tactile, temperature) |
| DV | Estimation error (estimate − actual) |
| Controls | Consistent environment, no visible clocks |

## Data Variables

| Variable | Type | Description | Range |
|----------|------|-------------|-------|
| `time_estimate_sec` | Continuous | 60-second estimation | ~30–90 sec |
| `line_a_estimate_cm` | Continuous | Line A length estimate | 1–25 cm |
| `line_b_estimate_cm` | Continuous | Line B length estimate | 1–25 cm |
| `string1_estimate_cm` | Continuous | String 1 estimate (tactile) | 1–40 cm |
| `string2_estimate_cm` | Continuous | String 2 estimate (tactile) | 1–40 cm |
| `temp_estimate_c` | Continuous | Room temperature guess | 15–30 °C |
| `time_counting` | Categorical | Counted during timing? | Yes steadily, Yes sometimes, No |
| `music_condition` | Categorical | Lab condition | silence, music |

## Calculated Variables (Error Scores)

| Variable | Formula | Interpretation |
|----------|---------|----------------|
| `time_error` | `time_estimate - 60` | + = overestimate (felt longer) |
| `line_a_error` | `estimate - actual` | + = thought longer than reality |
| `line_b_error` | `estimate - actual` | + = thought longer than reality |
| `string1_error` | `estimate - actual` | + = thought longer than reality |
| `string2_error` | `estimate - actual` | + = thought longer than reality |
| `temp_error` | `estimate - actual` | + = thought warmer than reality |

## Expected Results

| Measure | Typical Finding |
|---------|-----------------|
| 60-second estimation | Usually underestimate (say "stop" early) |
| Time error | Mean around −5 to −15 seconds |
| Visual vs tactile | Visual typically more accurate |
| Counters | More accurate than non-counters |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why Do We Underestimate Time?
When waiting without distraction, people often feel time passing more slowly than it actually is, leading them to say "stop" before 60 seconds have elapsed. This is called **temporal underestimation**.
:::

## Suggested Analyses

**Primary analyses:**

- **One-sample t-test**: Is mean time error different from 0?
- **Paired comparison**: Visual vs tactile estimation accuracy

**Descriptive statistics:**

- [Mean](../statistics/mean.qmd) and [SD](../statistics/standard-deviation.qmd) of each error score
- Proportion of over- vs under-estimators

**Exploratory analyses:**

- Does counting improve time estimation accuracy?
- Compare music vs silence conditions on time perception

## R Code Starter

```r
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate time error
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(time_error = time_estimate_sec - 60)

# One-sample t-test: Is mean error different from 0?
t.test(datalab$time_error, mu = 0)

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_under = mean(time_error < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Compare counters vs non-counters
datalab |>
  group_by(time_counting) |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Visualise time estimation
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = time_estimate_sec)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#275882", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Time Estimate (seconds)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "60-Second Estimation Distribution",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = actual 60 seconds"
  )
```

## Connection to Other Concepts

This station demonstrates:

- [Within-Groups Design](../design/within-groups-design.qmd) — same participant across multiple tasks
- [Mean](../statistics/mean.qmd) — calculating average error
- Testing against a hypothesised value (one-sample t-test)

## Tips for Facilitators

- Ensure participants **cannot see clocks or phones** during time estimation
- For tactile estimation, participants should keep eyes **fully closed**
- Note if participants use counting strategies — this is valuable data
- Actual measurements (line lengths, string lengths, room temp) should be recorded beforehand
